summary.text: A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.
General relativity predicts that any sufficiently compact mass forms one, with an event horizon marking the boundary of no escape and a central singularity.
They typically form when massive stars collapse in supernovae, can grow by absorbing matter, and are found through their effects on surrounding matter and light.

items.prompt: In 1784, John Michell reasoned that a star with the Sun's density but a vastly larger radius would be invisible. What was his argument?

options.label: It would collapse before it could shine
Its surface would hide light behind thick gas
Its gravity would bend all light into a ring
Its surface escape velocity would exceed light's speed

items.explain: He calculated that such a star's surface escape velocity would exceed the speed of light, so no emitted light would escape.

items.prompt: A black hole gives off no light of its own. How can astronomers still find one?

options.label: By how it affects nearby matter, light and orbiting stars
By the dark patch it casts on a telescope lens
By the heat it radiates into space
By direct photos of its inside

items.explain: Its presence can be inferred from interactions with matter and radiation, such as accretion disks or the orbits of stars.

items.prompt: An astronaut drifts across a black hole's event horizon. According to general relativity, what does she notice at that moment?

options.label: A sudden wall of intense light
Her clock stops ticking altogether
No local change, even though she is now trapped
A violent shove back out

items.explain: Crossing the event horizon traps an object but produces no locally detectable change.

items.prompt: How might a supermassive black hole end up with millions of solar masses?

options.label: By cooling until it stops radiating heat
By absorbing stars, merging, or gas collapse
By slowly gaining mass from its own light
By being born that size in a supernova

items.explain: They may form by absorbing stars, merging with other black holes, or via direct collapse of gas clouds.

items.prompt: Even small stellar black holes today take in mass from the cosmic microwave background faster than they lose it to Hawking radiation. What does that mean for them?

options.label: They are shrinking, though very slowly
They are growing instead of evaporating
They hold a perfectly constant mass
They are about to vanish

items.explain: Since the gain outpaces the loss, even the smallest observed black holes are gaining mass.

items.prompt: Karl Schwarzschild found a solution to Einstein's equations that became singular at a certain radius. How did early physicists react?

options.label: They quickly accepted it as the edge of a black hole
They understood it at once as an event horizon
They tested it with telescopes
Its nature was not understood, and many doubted black holes existed

items.explain: The meaning of that radius was not understood at the time, and many early physicists were sceptical of black holes.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing gets out
paragraphs.text: A black hole is an object in space packed so tightly that its gravity lets nothing escape, not even light. Einstein's general relativity, which treats gravity as curved spacetime, predicts that any mass squeezed small enough will become one. The edge past which there is no way back is called the event horizon. Crossing it traps an object inside, yet according to the theory nothing noticeable happens to that object at the moment it crosses.

paragraphs.heading: A point of infinite curvature
paragraphs.text: General relativity also says every black hole should hold a central singularity, a place where the curvature of spacetime becomes infinite. For a long time black holes were seen as a mathematical oddity. Only in the 1960s did theoretical work show that the theory predicts them as a general result rather than a special case.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea
paragraphs.text: The thought of a body whose pull holds back light goes back to the late 18th century. The English astronomer and clergyman John Michell, and separately the French scientist Pierre-Simon Laplace, both pictured very large stars rather than the tiny, dense objects of the modern idea. In a letter published in 1784, Michell worked out that a star as dense as the Sun but 500 times wider would trap its own light, since escaping its surface would need more than light speed. He also guessed, correctly, that such dark bodies might be found by their pull on visible neighbours.

paragraphs.heading: From Schwarzschild to Cygnus X-1
paragraphs.text: A few months after Einstein published his field equations, the astrophysicist Karl Schwarzschild applied them to a star, assuming it was a perfect sphere that did not spin. At a certain distance from the centre, his solution became singular, meaning some terms went to infinity. That distance, later named the Schwarzschild radius, was not understood at the time, and many physicists doubted black holes were real. By the late 1950s the solution was being read as a region nothing can leave, and between 1971 and 1974 the X-ray source Cygnus X-1 became the first black hole most astronomers accepted.

paragraphs.heading: How they form and grow
paragraphs.text: Black holes usually form in a supernova, when a massive star collapses at the end of its life. Once formed, a black hole can grow by taking in mass from around it. Supermassive black holes, millions of times the Sun's mass, may build up by swallowing stars and merging with other black holes, or by gas clouds collapsing directly. Astronomers agree that most galaxies have one at their centre.

paragraphs.heading: Finding something you cannot see
paragraphs.text: A black hole shows itself through what it does to matter and light nearby. Matter falling in can form an accretion disk, a swirl of hot plasma heated by friction that glows; in extreme cases this makes a quasar, among the brightest objects in the universe. Merging black holes give off gravitational waves that can be detected. Stars orbiting a black hole reveal its mass and position, and this is how astronomers found that Sagittarius A*, at the heart of the Milky Way, holds a black hole of about 4.3 million solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: Slowly glowing away
paragraphs.text: When quantum field theory is worked out in curved spacetime, it predicts that an event horizon gives off Hawking radiation, and the smaller the black hole, the faster it radiates. If it is not taking in matter, this makes the black hole lose mass very slowly. In practice, even stellar black holes, the smallest kind observed, gain more mass from the cosmic microwave background than they lose this way.
